analysis.one_liner: Ends the corporate tax deduction for executive pay exceeding 25 times the lowest-paid worker.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in October 2007 with 27 Democratic cosponsors and died in the Ways and Means Committee without ever getting a House vote [S1][S4][S5].
analysis.plain_summary: Under current tax law, companies can deduct executive salaries, bonuses, and benefits as a business expense, which lowers their taxes and effectively subsidizes very large pay packages [S3]. This bill would deny that deduction for any employee paid more than 25 times the company's lowest-paid full-time worker, and require companies that cross that line to report their lowest, average, and top pay to the Treasury [S2][S3]. Companies could still pay executives anything they wanted; they would just stop getting taxpayers to help pick up the tab [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, because companies would no longer get a federal tax write-off for outsized executive pay, and workers would gain visibility into pay gaps through the required reporting [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and workers facing pay gaps

how_it_helps.text: Companies could no longer deduct compensation above 25 times their lowest-paid full-time employee's pay, ending a federal tax subsidy for extreme pay ratios [S3].

Employers who pay anyone more than 25 times their lowest-paid worker would have to report that worker's pay, average non-managerial pay, average executive pay, and the exact pay of the top five employees to the Treasury, making pay gaps public [S3].
The change would apply to taxable years after enactment, so it would take effect immediately once signed into law [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations with highly paid executives, which would owe more federal tax because part of that pay would no longer count as a deductible business expense [S3].

drawbacks.text: Companies could restructure pay to avoid the rule, for example by shifting executives to contractors or adjusting how lowest-paid workers are counted, and enforcement would depend on new Treasury reporting rules [S3].

The deduction limit applies only to salary, wages, bonuses, and noncash benefits, so other forms of executive compensation could still be deductible, and the bill does not directly cap anyone's pay [S3].
Higher tax bills for affected companies are a real cost, and some economists argue limits on executive pay deductions can push compensation into harder-to-tax forms rather than reduce it [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: companies with extreme pay gaps would pay more tax, and the public would stop subsidizing the highest paychecks, while gaining pay-ratio data it does not currently get [S2][S3]. The bill is narrow — it caps a deduction, not pay itself, and companies could still pay executives whatever the market bears — so its effect on actual pay gaps would likely be modest, but the cost is limited to the corporations that cross the 25-to-1 line [S3].

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Ways and Means Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Barbara Lee introduced the Income Equity Act of 2007 in the House on October 17, 2007 [S1][S5].
The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the same day and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote [S5].
Twenty-six Democratic representatives cosponsored the bill; no Republican did [S4].
The Congress ended on January 3, 2009, and the bill was never reported out of committee, so it died [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporations paying executives far more than 25 times their lowest-paid workers kept a tax deduction worth billions, and executives kept the taxpayer-subsidized status quo. Working people gained nothing, since the bill never got a vote.

for.role: Original cosponsors, U.S. House of Representatives

against.name: Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled [S5].

sides.party_line_note: All 27 supporters — the sponsor and 26 cosponsors — were Democrats, and no Republican cosponsored; the bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call record exists [S4].

industries.industry: Large corporations with highly paid executives
industries.note: They would lose the tax deduction for any pay above 25 times their lowest-paid worker's, raising their federal tax bills [S3]. The deduction is a direct federal subsidy for extreme pay ratios, so ending it runs against the interest of companies with the largest pay gaps and alongside ordinary taxpayers'.

Executive pay itself would not be capped, but the loss of the deduction would create pressure to keep top salaries within the 25-to-1 line or restructure them, changing the market for pay design [S3].
